_comment: Conversations this deployment actually produced, kept so that a change to
the prompt can be judged against real answers rather than invented ones.
Taken from /api/contributions, which only returns conversations contributed
with consent. No identifiers are stored, so these cannot be linked to a
person. The answers are the owner's own test runs.
Why a replay is worth having, and what it cannot tell you. The answers
here were given to the OLD questions. Replay them against a new prompt and
turn one is a fair comparison - the opening account is the same - while
every later answer is a reply to a question that was not asked. So a
replay is a test of how the questions READ and whether they presuppose,
not a test of how a conversation GOES. For the second thing there is no

conversations.name: Soho recommendation, no way to judge it
conversations.note: The conversation that prompted the question rewrite. Five of six questions presupposed a deficit; the sixth asked what the system could have known and got the only answer that named the gap.
answers: I was using it to recommend me for a restaurant/ pub near soho
I cannot weigh, I'm new to the place. But once I got the recommendation, I asked someone they said yeah it's a cool place
It said me that it's a nice place with lot of young woman. Not too crowdy so can find time for introductions etc
That's AI reasoning, i wouldn't know much
questions: What did you weigh that recommendation against before deciding where to actually go?
What did that person actually know about the place—had they been there recently, or were they just going on reputation?
What was riding on this choice—were you going for a casual drink or something like marking an occasion—if the place had turned out wrong for that?
If the place had turned out to be the wrong vibe for that, what would that have cost you that evening?
Beyond picking a name for you, what did it actually tell you about the place that you couldn't have found yourself with a quick search?
Where would that read on the young-woman, not-too-crowded part have come from—what could it have actually known about that place's crowd on a given night?

conversations.name: Which of 400 roles to apply for
conversations.note: Ran to the turn cap with no reflection, although the last answer names the gap outright - a reference he could give that the system could not know about, and a role closed internally that it could not see.
answers: I was looking to use ai to  help me decide which of these 400 roles I can apply
I didn't yet apply yet, but I gave detail profile history, my personal preferences, all info about my background etc
I didn't understand the question, it has everything it needs about those roles like jd, company etc. What else does it need?
They are accurate. That's not the concern
Well, i would probably apply for the ones I am not qualified or not apply for the ones I'm qualified

Manually verify, if it over shot or under shot a role. I mean, said am not qualified for a role based one it's matching criteria but probably i might have a reference to give it a shot it wouldn't know. Or something it thinks am qualified but the role might be too popular and might have been closed internally
questions: What did you ask it to use in narrowing down those 400 roles, and what happened once you applied that shortlist?
Beyond what you gave it about yourself, what did it actually have about the 400 roles themselves to judge fit against?
Where did those job descriptions and company details come from, and how recent or accurate did you confirm them to be?
What did you actually compare those listings against to confirm they were accurate and current?
What would happen to your job search if the shortlist it produced turned out to be wrong for you in some way you hadn't yet spotted?
What would you actually need to see to catch a case where it called you qualified or unqualified wrongly, before you acted on that call?
